CA.note: Section 671's Testudines entries reach only Chelydridae (snapping turtles). No tortoise family is restricted, and California's own tortoise rules concern the native desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) as a protected species, not an exotic-possession restriction.

NY.note: No tortoise or Testudinidae entry appears anywhere in the closed dangerous-wild-animal definition, which among reptiles names only certain large monitors, big constrictors, venomous species and crocodilians.

MA.note: Massachusetts allows all species of turtles (up to 100 individuals/eggs per species) without a permit except five named exceptions: Argentina/Chaco tortoise, Gopherus spp. (gopher tortoises), pancake tortoise, spotted turtle, and red-eared slider. The red-footed tortoise is not among them.

NJ.note: Not on the exempt-species list (N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4), which names only American anole, common iguana, boa constrictor, eastern painted turtle, snapping turtle, fence lizard, garter snake, tokay gecko and ribbon snake among reptiles. Falls to the § 4.5 catch-all: 'a permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians... not specifically exempted.'

VA.note: No tortoise, Chelonoidis, or Testudinidae entry appears in the nonnative-animal permit table. Subsection (H) allows possession of nonnative animals not listed in the table, subject to general law.

GA.note: Georgia's licensed wild-animal reptile list names only two turtles (African helmeted turtle, Chinese softshell turtle) under Order Testudines; no tortoise or Testudinidae entry appears.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: A tortoise is a turtle in the taxonomic sense the category uses (Order Testudines), the same reading applied to the sulcata and Russian tortoise.

RI.quote: All exotic species of turtles may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit, except endangered species.
RI.note: The three tortoises pulled back out are the Chaco tortoise, the genus Gopherus and the pancake tortoise. Chelonoidis carbonarius is none of them and is not federally endangered.

FL.note: Not on Florida's prohibited reptile list (sixteen high-risk species, no tortoise) and not a Class I or II wildlife species requiring a specific license.

TX.note: Not on Texas's closed dangerous-wild-animal list (lions, tigers, and other named cats, bears, canids and primates). Tortoises and monitor lizards are outside the registration requirement.

LA.note: Absent from Louisiana's prohibited and restricted nonnative-reptile lists (which do name the savannah and Nile monitor). The native-turtle registration requirement at § 101.G governs Louisiana's own species and does not reach this South American tortoise.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of turtles with a carapace or shell length of more than 4 inches and not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(ix) Testudinidae (tortoises);
MT.note: Cleared by family, above the four-inch floor, the same basis already used for the sulcata and Russian tortoise.

MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is drawn family by family and is entirely mammalian; no reptile is restricted under this rule at any size.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captive-wildlife chapter or current administrative rules.

KS.note: Kansas's only exotic-pet statute reaches six named cats, bears, and non-native venomous snakes. Tortoises are untouched at any size.

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute covers venomous reptiles and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

KY.note: On neither the prohibited species list nor the inherently-dangerous list, which among reptiles names only gila monsters, beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, crocodilians and venomous snakes other than hognose.

WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians.

IA.note: The squamate/reptile half of Iowa's dangerous-wild-animal definition is exhaustively enumerated (certain monitors, helodermatids, venomous snakes, three named giant constrictors). No tortoise is among them.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only (carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants, primates); reptiles fall under Game, Fish and Parks rules instead.

MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so outside Class I, and not a deadly or dangerous reptile over eight feet under § 578.023.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Non-venomous and not on the prohibited list, so no permit is required for personal use; the reptile must remain confined and never be released.

NH.quote: (4) Non-venomous reptiles, except the following: a. Indigenous reptile species listed in Table 800.1...
NH.note: No tortoise appears anywhere in the controlled table, so this non-native species clears the non-controlled category outright.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: A conventional pet under the reptile category, no size or weight qualifier attached.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: No permit required; the clean list sets no size limit on reptiles.

OH.note: Not a dangerous wild animal and not native to Ohio, so nothing in Chapter 935 reaches it.

WA.quote: Class reptilia ... Order crocodilia, all species
WA.note: Not listed. Washington's reptile concerns under this chapter are venom and crocodilians rather than size or origin.

ME.note: Maine's own tortoise clearance list (documented in this site's sulcata-tortoise research) names the Russian, Greek, Hermann's, leopard, red-footed and yellow-footed tortoises by common name. The red-footed tortoise is expressly included; the exact binomial spelling used on Maine's PDF was not independently re-verified this round because the source PDF resisted text extraction, so double-check the primary document (maine.gov/ifw/docs/unrestrictedspecies.pdf) before publishing.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Tortoises (Genera: Agrionemys, Aldabrachelys, Chelonoidis, Centrochelys, Geochelone, Gopherus, Indotestudo, Manouria, Psuedotestudo, Stigmochelys, Testudo)
AR.note: Confirmed directly from the current AGFC PDF (revised 11/1/22). Genus Chelonoidis is named outright, which covers the red-footed tortoise without ambiguity.

HI.cite: List of Conditionally Approved Animals, Family Testudinidae
HI.quote: Chelonoidis (all species in genus except C. elephantopus)
HI.note: Confirmed directly from the HDOA conditional-animal-list PDF. Unlike the sulcata (which moved out of Geochelone entirely into the unlisted genus Centrochelys, leaving its status genuinely unclear), the red-footed tortoise's current genus Chelonoidis is named outright on this list, with only the Galapagos tortoise (C. elephantopus, separately restricted) carved out. Chelonoidis carbonarius is squarely covered.
